With this motivation in mind we will show in this paper that gauge invariance could be considered an emergent concept having its origin in the algebraic formalism of a well known method that deals with constrained systems, namely, the Faddeev-Jackiw (FJ) technique. input: How do modality constraints in CSA systems, as informed by foundational work on human-computer interaction, impact the design and user experience of these systems?
expected_output: The modality constraints in Conversational Search Agent (CSA) systems significantly impact the design and user experience of these systems, as informed by foundational work on human-computer interaction. For instance, a voice-only CSA, due to its limited and serial bandwidth, requires the agent to be sensitive to the constraints of speech, resulting in shorter responses. In contrast, a multi-modal CSA can present more detailed and combined responses, such as a search engine result page with query suggestions and facets. Additionally, a chat-based CSA, while having restrictions on screen space and bandwidth, benefits from a persistent conversation, allowing users to refer back to previous options. These modality constraints influence the cost of different conversational turns, affecting the user's accumulated gain from the conversation, and ultimately shaping the design and user experience of CSA systems to balance gain and cost.
actual_output: Modality constraints in CSA systems, informed by foundational work on human-computer interaction, prioritize user needs over algorithmic proficiency by designing systems that match human cognition and mental models, as advocated by human-computer interaction principles [1]. This human-centered design approach focuses on making systems more acceptable and benevolent, considering factors such as user satisfaction, expertise, and mental models, ultimately enhancing the overall usability and user experience of these systems [1]. The impact of modality constraints on user experience is further influenced by the dynamic cycle of perception and action, where the information needed to guide upcoming actions is informed by user behavior, such as where they look and how they move, shaping the environment and changing the perceptual experience [2]. In the context of mobile devices, which are characterized by their size, reduced processing power, and input modalities, the design of CSA systems must also consider these unique factors to optimize user experience, as investigated in research on mobile geospatial applications [3].

Paper: Dynamics of eye-hand coordination are flexibly preserved in eye-cursor coordination during an online, digital, object interaction task
Section: Introduction

At the core of all well-considered user experiences is the user themselves. So-called human-centered designs incorporate behaviour, cognition, and perception into their product. An early example is the psychophysical mapping of human sensitivity to flickering light. Over hundreds of years, scientists learned that a light display refreshing at a minimum of 30 Hz appeared continuous to the human eye - setting the benchmark for early computer screens.Of course, perceiving the world is only part of a user’s experience - they also interact with their environment to achieve their goals. Like the display refresh-rate example, principles of human interaction can dictate good design. Fitts’ Law is one such finding that is now adopted as a design principle in human-computer interaction (HCI) , . In this seminal work, Fitts quantified the speed-accuracy tradeoff for movements of different amplitudes (how far you need to move) to targets of different sizes . Put succinctly, he showed a lawful relationship whereby larger amplitude movements and smaller targets both result in longer movement times. These real-world findings have since been explored in depth in an HCI context, informing and assessing the design of two- and three-dimensional pointing devices, the soft (virtual) QWERTY keyboard, and the properties and placement of interactive web elements, .Critically, user experience (UX) is best thought of as a dynamic cycle of perception and action whereby the information we need to guide our upcoming actions is informed by where we look; how we move then shapes the environment causing changes in the perceptual experience. Consider, for example, the coordinated effort required of the visual and motor systems to safely pick up a cup full of hot coffee. Before any movement, the eyes will fixate the drink, leading the action of the hand by about 500 milliseconds. Seamlessly, as soon as the mug is grasped, the eyes will move to look at the next object for action, like a sugar packet, well before the hand is finished moving the hot drink . These patterns of visuomotor coordination are ubiquitous and stereotypic, appearing in human and non-human primates , alike. Here we ask, in the same way real-world findings have informed computer screen and keyboard design, can principles of real-world eye-hand coordination help inform UX design for digital interactions?To approach this question, we used an online, eye-tracking-enabled platform (Labvanced; ) to create a screen-based version of a real-world object interaction task . Instead of moving cups to targets on a table, crowdsourced participants (N = 51) dragged circles to targets on their computer screen while we recorded cursor movements and webcam eye-gaze coordinates. For BIPs, efficiency and accuracy are the primary influences of their popularity in science and engineering. input: What causes coherences to affect quantum work definitions, leading to impacts on fluctuation theorems?
expected_output: The presence of coherences in the energy eigenbasis affects the definition of quantum work because the two projective energy measurement scheme, which is commonly used to define quantum work, does not possess some desired properties when applied to initial states with coherences. This is due to the fact that the two projective energy measurement scheme is based on the idea of measuring the energy of the system before and after a process, but when the system is in a coherent state, the energy measurement can disturb the system and affect the outcome. As a result, there is an ongoing debate about the proper definition of quantum work in the presence of coherences, which in turn impacts the verification of fluctuation theorems, as these theorems rely on a well-defined notion of work.
actual_output: Quantum coherence affects quantum work definitions because the standard definition of quantum fluctuating work, based on the two-projective energy measurement, does not apply to systems with initial quantum coherence, as the first projective energy measurement destroys the initial coherence [1]. This destruction of quantum coherence by projective measurements means that the first law of thermodynamics cannot be satisfied, highlighting the challenge of defining work in the quantum regime, where work is not an observable [2][3]. Evidence suggests that quantum coherence makes the resulting coherent work highly susceptible to changes in energy level structure and enhances quantum fluctuations, enabling them to overcome thermal fluctuations and revive symmetry-breaking transitions [4]. As a result, in the presence of quantum coherence, work and its fluctuation can exhibit critical behavior even at high temperature, and work fluctuation in the ferromagnetism regime is significantly decreased by quantum coherence, while average work can be either increased or decreased depending on relative phase [5][6].

The concept of work is one of the cornerstones of thermodynamics. To extend it and its fluctuation theorems to the quantum domain is of fundamental importance in quantum thermodynamics. Different from the classical case, it is very hard to define work in the quantum regime, because work is not an observable . Traditionally, to determine the work in the quantum regime one needs to perform two projective energy measurement (TPM) at the beginning and the end of the external protocol , . Based on TPM, the quantum extension of fluctuation theorems is obtained, see the reviews , for detail discussion, and these fluctuation theorems have been experimentally verified in various systems, . However, the initial quantum coherence is destroyed by the first measurement, and therefore the work fluctuation relation obtained by TPM is not “quantum" to some extent. And due to the severe impact of projective measurement on the system dynamics, the first law of thermodynamics can not be satisfied.In order to include the effects of initial quantum coherence, a lot of efforts have been made. Replacing projective measurement by weak measurement, a part of quantum coherence can be preserved, but the impact of measurement can not be eliminated. Analogy to classical trajectory in phase space, Sampaio et al. gave the quantum trajectory using quantum Hamilton-Jacobi theory, and defined work as the power integrated along the trajectory . In fact, for a work distribution including initial coherence the first law of thermodynamics and nonequilibrium fluctuation theorem are mutually exclusive, . Quasi-static decay refers to the slow relaxation process that occurs in a system when it is driven at a shear rate smaller than the inverse relaxation time, which is a common scenario in many experimental situations. This approach ignores the "fast" wing of the relaxation spectrum, which would take place in real experiments at a finite value of the shear rate. In contrast, non-affine decay is associated with the correlations of the non-affine displacement field, which can be analyzed by computing the correlation function. The non-affine correlation field exhibits a decay over a typical length of 23 particle sizes, followed by a negative tail, indicating anti-correlation. The quasi-static procedure ensures that after a local "bond" breaks, new bonds can form instantaneously, whereas the non-affine decay is related to the organization of the non-affine deformation in "vortices". The effects of these mechanisms on material properties are significant, as they can influence the elastic character of the response, the relaxation times, and the correlations of the displacement field. Overall, the quasi-static decay and non-affine decay are interconnected, and understanding their underlying mechanisms is crucial for describing the plastic response of glassy systems.

However, the exploration of these properties is often hindered by the challenges of measuring and controlling forces at the nanoscale, as well as the inherent stochasticity of biomolecular interactions. Furthermore, the application of theoretical frameworks, such as the Jarzynski relation, to describe non-equilibrium processes in biomolecular systems can be limited by the complexity of these systems and the difficulty of obtaining accurate measurements. Additionally, the use of biomolecules as nanotools requires a deep understanding of their statistical mechanical properties, which can be difficult to quantify and control, particularly in small system sizes. Overall, while biomolecules' physical properties hold great promise for optimizing nanotool performance, their limitations must be carefully considered and addressed through continued research and development.

Section: Introduction

Bayesian methods provide a way to expand scalar predictions to full posterior probabilities .

The property of scale equivariance impacts the optimization process by allowing the model to generalize well over different scales, which is demonstrated through the comparison of feature maps of specific layers using the norm for two differently scaled inputs. Additionally, the use of Adam enables faster progress in terms of both the number of iterations and wall-clock time, outperforming other optimizers such as the sum-of-functions method, and shows better convergence than other stochastic first-order methods on multi-layer neural networks trained with dropout noise. The update rule for Adam involves computing bias-corrected moment estimates and combines adaptive step-size strategies with momentum, acting as a diagonal preconditioner for gradient steps, which can mitigate the effect of the choice of certain hyperparameters on training loss optimization [4][5]. The Adam (Adaptive Moment Estimation) optimizer is a popular optimization algorithm for training deep neural networks, introduced by Kingma et al . It is an extension of the stochastic gradient descent (SGD) algorithm that adapts the learning rate for each parameter individually, based on the first and second moments of the gradients. This adaptive learning rate approach allows the optimizer to converge faster and achieve better performance compared to standard SGD. The Adam optimizer computes the first moment (mean) and the second moment (uncentered variance) of the gradients using exponential moving averages. It then corrects the bias in these moment estimates and updates the parameters using the corrected moments. The update rule for each parameter can be expressed as:\begin{split}

v_t &= \beta _2 v_{t-1} + (1 - \beta _2) g_t^2, \\

input: How does exergy loss compare to electromagnetic inertia in terms of energy efficiency in systems where both phenomena are present?
expected_output: Exergy loss and electromagnetic inertia are two distinct concepts that affect energy efficiency in systems where both phenomena are present. Exergy loss refers to the destruction of the maximum available work that can be extracted from a system in disequilibrium with its environment, which is intimately related to entropy generation. On the other hand, electromagnetic inertia is a concept that suggests the inertia of a body may have an electromagnetic origin. In terms of energy efficiency, exergy loss is a measure of the irreversibility of a system, which leads to a decrease in the system's ability to perform work. In contrast, electromagnetic inertia is a fundamental property that affects the behavior of particles and systems, but it does not directly relate to energy efficiency. However, if the force of gravitation has an electromagnetic origin, as suggested by some theories, then the gravitational field would be much weaker, which could lead to a more energy-efficient system. Nevertheless, the relationship between exergy loss and electromagnetic inertia in terms of energy efficiency is still a topic of ongoing research and debate, and more studies are needed to fully understand their interplay.
actual_output: Exergy loss is a primary concern in terms of energy efficiency in systems where both exergy loss and electromagnetic inertia are present, as the availability destruction in the Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) due to combustion reactions accounts for a significant portion of the total loss [1]. expected_output: Evaluating community detection via unbiased indices when the true partitions are unknown can be achieved through several methods. One approach is to use the Pearson correlation coefficient between incidence vectors, which is an unbiased similarity index. This can be computed in two ways: Pearson-sub, which only uses pairs from the set of nodes that participated in cascades, and Pearson-all, which is computed on the whole dataset. Another method is to restrict the ground truth partition only to the set of nodes that participated in cascades, or to extend the obtained partition from this set to the whole network, for example, by assigning all nodes in the unknown set to one cluster or to individual clusters. Additionally, local methods can create a binary partition of the network into the community itself and the remaining non-community nodes, and the accuracy of the found communities can be quantified by the fraction of correctly identified nodes, although this has been shown to have drawbacks. To overcome these limitations, a composite score can be used, which assigns a reward for each correct node and a penalty for each incorrect node, allowing for a more nuanced evaluation of community detection algorithms.

Additionally, methods such as the Adjusted Omega Index can be employed when the number of communities in the compared partitions are different, providing a comprehensive evaluation framework for community detection algorithms [3]. Validation metrics like NMI and ARI enable the comparison of results from different community detection methods, allowing for the identification of different types of partitions and the discovery of network structures when no a-priori information is available [4].

ResNet, short for Residual Network, was introduced by He et al. in their 2015 paper . This deep learning model, distinguished by its "skip" or "shortcut" connections, was developed to address the problem of vanishing gradients that plagued training of very deep neural networks. These shortcut connections allow the model to learn identity functions that effectively prevent the higher layers from destroying the learned information of lower layers, thereby enabling the successful training of networks that are significantly deeper than those previously possible. ResNet has had a significant impact on the field of computer vision, including the domain of super-resolution. SRResNet, or Super-Resolution Residual Network, is a direct adaptation of the principles of ResNet to super-resolution tasks. SRResNet was proposed by Ledig et al. in the SRGAN (Super-Resolution Generative Adversarial Networks) paper and serves as the backbone for the generator network in SRGAN . SRResNet incorporates residual blocks to learn the residual mapping between the low-resolution and high-resolution images. It is designed with a shallow network at the beginning and end (for feature extraction and reconstruction) while having a deeper body composed of residual blocks. Building upon the success of SRResNet, researchers proposed an enhanced version known as Enhanced SRResNet (ESRResNet) . The enhanced version incorporates several advancements in deep learning, like the use of dense connections (as seen in DenseNet ) and parameter-efficient convolutions to improve the network's learning capacity while keeping the computational load manageable. In addition, one key feature of the ESRResNet is the use of Residual-in-Residual Dense Blocks (RRDBs) instead of the simple residual blocks in the original SRResNet. The RRDB is essentially a stack of residual blocks where the output of each residual block is added to its input (forming a local skip connection), and the output of the last residual block in the stack is also added to the input of the stack (forming a long skip connection). This architecture allows for better propagation of features and gradients through the network, making it easier for the network to learn the mapping from low-resolution to high-resolution images. The idea is to generalize the “single-step” version of Lobato (1999)'s GSE considered in Shimotsu (2007) by substituting the periodogram function, applied in defining the estimator's objective function, by an arbitrary estimator of the spectral density. Although a useful tool in spectral analysis, it is well-known that the periodogram is an ill-behaved inconsistent estimator of the spectral density. Seen as a random variable, it does not even converge to a random variable at all (cf. We show the consistency of the GSE obtained under the same conditions in the process as considered in Shimotsu (2007). Second, we relax the consistency condition by considering spectral density estimators satisfying certain mild moment conditions and show the consistency of the related estimator. Third we examine the asymptotic normality of the proposed estimator under a certain mild regularity condition on the spectral density estimator and under the same assumptions as in Shimotsu (2007). This suggests that the influence of type Ia supernovae on star formation processes varies across different gas density environments, with lower densities being more susceptible to the disruptive effects of these explosions.

By means of 3D hydrodynamic simulations, we study how Type Ia supernovae
(SNe) explosions affect the star formation history and the chemical properties
of second generation (SG) stars in globular clusters (GC). SG stars are assumed

the low-density scenario with short delay time, the explosions start at the

weakly affected by SN explosions, with a final SG mass similar to the one
obtained without SNe Ia. Most of the stars form from a mix of AGB ejecta and
pristine gas and have a modest helium enrichment. We show that gas from SNe Ia

Quantum Fisher Information (QFI) is an important concept of Quantum estimation theory (QET), a direct extension of the classical estimation theory . In QET, it sets up a lower bound for the estimation of parameters, which are not directly accessible to measurements and potentially affect the dynamics of different physical quantities of interest, . Besides QET, it has numerous uses in other fields based on the applications of quantum mechanics. For example, in quantum information theory, it is used as a tool for measuring non-Markovianity of environments, quantum entanglement of many-body systems, quantum phase transition and distinguishability of quantum states on Hilbert spaces, .A frequent strategy for studying the dynamics of QFI and using it as a tool for either estimating some unknown parameters or other characteristics of the environment is to monitor the evolution of an open quantum probe. Generally, a small controlled quantum system, usually a qubit, is allowed to interact with a bigger uncontrolled system (environment). During the interaction between the two, the information about the unknown parameter of the environment is encoded onto the space of the qubit. This encoded piece of information is then revealed through studying the dynamics of QFI which, in turn, enables for employing the estimation procedure. This strategy is very successful in studying the behavior of QFI under various setups. For instance, its dynamics provides useful information about the effects of single bosonic environment, multiple bosonic environments , and about the cutoff frequency of Ohmic type bosonic environments .In quantum thermodynamics, QFI has a pivotal role in estimating optimal temperature for different quantum mechanical processes, . Many recent studies have focused on the measurement of temperature at very small scales in which nano-sized thermal environments are considered. The temperature of such environments become very sensitive to the disturbances caused by the presence of quantum probes, . Quantum harmonic oscillators , atomic condensates , and nanomechanical resonators are some interesting paradigms of nanoscale thermometry. In modern science and technology, precise estimation of optimal temperature has great significance on experimental realizations of many devices, .In this paper, we study the dynamics of QFI as a function of temperature, time of interaction, squeezing amplitude and phase parameter for an exactly solvable model of a squeezed thermal environment interacting with a single qubit. This transformation allows for the connection of MFG and SB frameworks through PDEs, which can be seen in the coincidence of the agent's dynamic with the forward SDE in SB. In practice, this transformation can improve the performance of MFG models by providing a more accurate and efficient way of solving Stochastic Balance Problems (SBPs) with gradient and mixed-conservative dissipative drifts. Additionally, the transformation helps to ensure the convergence of the recursion used in the computational framework, which is contractive in Hilbert's projective metric under certain assumptions. Variational Monte Carlo (VMC) methods are a family of computational methods that do not suffer from the sign problem and whose computational cost is tractable.
In particular, VMC combines a variational encoding of the wave function, to reduce the memory complexity associated with storing the wave function, with Monte Carlo techniques which lower the computational complexity.

where representing uncertainty is of crucial importance, such as automated driving  and healthcare .Some recent efforts have been made towards improving the robustness of deep neural networks against adversarial samples by doing adversarial training , reverse cross-entropy training  or Bayesian averaging .
On the other hand, the probabilistic view of machine learning offers mathematically grounded tools for dealing with uncertainty, i.e., Bayesian methods . Bayesian methods also provide a theoretically sound approach to incorporating structural bias  and domain knowledge as prior or posterior constraints  to achieve efficient learning with a small number of training samples. Thus it is beneficial to combine the complimentary advantages of deep learning and Bayesian methods, which in fact has been drawing tremendous attention in recent years .Moreover, as most of the success in deep learning comes from supervised tasks that require a large number of labeled data, research in this area is paying more and more attention to unsupervised learning, a long-standing goal of artificial intelligence (AI). Probabilistic models and Bayesian methods are commonly treated as principled approaches to modeling unlabeled data for pure unsupervised learning or its hybrid with supervised learning (aka., semi-supervised learning). Recently, the popularity of deep generative models again demonstrates the promise of combining deep neural networks with probabilistic modeling, which has shown superior results in image generation, semi-supervised classification , and one-shot learning .We call such an arising direction that conjoins the advantages of Bayesian methods and deep learning as Bayesian Deep Learning (BDL). The scope of BDL covers the traditional Bayesian methods, the deep learning methods where probabilistic inference plays a key role, and their intersection. One unique feature of BDL is that the deterministic transformation between random variables can be automatically learned from data under an expressive parametric formulation typically using deep neural networks , while in traditional Bayesian models, the transformation tends to have a simple analytical form (e.g., the exponential function or inner product). One key challenge for Bayesian deep learning is on posterior inference, which is typically intractable for such models and needs sophisticated approximation techniques. Although much progress has been made on both variational inference and Monte Carlo methods , it is still too difficult for practitioners to pick-up. Moreover, although variational inference and Monte Carlo methods have their general recipes, it is still quite involved for an experienced researcher to derive the equations and implement every detail for a particular model.

Section: Conclusions

We perform radiative transfer simulations for the newly discovered TRAPPIST-1 planets, under the assumption that each may have an atmosphere similar to that of present-day Earth. We find that the biosignature ozone, at present-day Earth levels, could be detectable for TRAPPIST-1b with at least 60 transits each with NIRSpec and MIRI, and for 1c and 1b with 30 transits. TRAPPIST-1d, as the coolest planet in the system, is most likely to be habitable and therefore have substantial amounts of ozone; however, this planet is currently thought to have an 18-day orbit, and the system is far from the continuous viewing zone for JWST, meaning that 30 transits with each instrument would take 10 years to obtain. input: How does the impact of magnetic fields on pinning frequency differ between weak and strong WC superconductors, and what underlying mechanisms from existing research on WC materials contribute to these differences?
expected_output: The impact of magnetic fields on pinning frequency differs between weak and strong WC superconductors due to the distinct underlying mechanisms. In weak WC superconductors, the pinning frequency is controlled by the lengthscale associated with the threshold force, which is naturally associated with pinning. This lengthscale depends on the size of the particle, and as a result, the pinning frequency exhibits additional magnetic field dependence, particularly in the case of strong magnetic fields where the cyclotron orbit plays a significant role. In contrast, strong WC superconductors exhibit a different behavior, with the pinning frequency being influenced by the presence of topological defects, such as dislocations, which occur at a larger lengthscale. The elastic theory, which is more stable to the presence of topological defects than initially anticipated, can reliably compute the characteristics of the peak and above, and thus most of the a.c. transport, but dislocations will spoil the results of the elastic theory for the optical conductivity only well below the peak. Existing research on WC materials suggests that the magnetic field not only confines the electrons but also plays a crucial role in determining the response of the system to disorder, allowing for the possibility of observing novel field dependences.
actual_output: The impact of magnetic fields on pinning frequency differs between weak and strong WC superconductors, with the pinning frequency increasing with increasing magnetic field in experiments, which contradicts naive expectations based on Fukuyama-Lee arguments that the pinning frequency decreases with increasing magnetic field [1]. In the pinned Wigner crystal (WC) approach, if field-independent elastic constants are assumed, a reduction of the spectral weight in the pinning peak is expected due to continuous transfer of spectral weight from the pinning peak at low frequencies to the cyclotron peak, but this is not observed in experiments [1]. The experimental systems lie in the strong field regime where the condition allows for the pinning frequency to increase with magnetic field, and at low temperatures and high magnetic fields, vortex viscosity is suppressed, which modifies the properties of high-Tc superconductors [2][3]. The crossover from weak- to strong bulk pinning is triggered either by increasing the strength of the defect potential or by decreasing the effective elasticity of the lattice, which affects the pinning frequency and the behavior of the superconductor [4].

input: How can repulsive forces in microscopic models be utilized to improve the accuracy of pedestrian flow simulations in real-world scenarios?
expected_output: In microscopic models, such as the social force model, repulsive forces can be utilized to improve the accuracy of pedestrian flow simulations by accounting for the influence of walls and other obstacles on pedestrian motion. The repulsive force can be modeled as a potential that pedestrians experience when approaching a wall, which can be calibrated using experimental data. By incorporating this repulsive force into the simulation, researchers can better capture the behavior of pedestrians in real-world scenarios, such as navigating through crowded areas or avoiding collisions with walls or other pedestrians. Additionally, the repulsive force can be used to model the interaction between pedestrians and walls in a more realistic way, taking into account the shape and size of the wall, as well as the pedestrian's velocity and direction. This can lead to more accurate predictions of pedestrian flow and behavior in complex environments.
actual_output: Repulsive forces in microscopic models, such as the social-force model (SFM), can be utilized to improve the accuracy of pedestrian flow simulations by modeling the collision-avoidance performed by pedestrians [1][2]. The SFM, which describes the movement of pedestrians by means of repulsive forces that decay exponentially with distance, has been widely used to study pedestrian dynamics in various settings and can be calibrated using experimental measurements to adjust the repulsive force [1]. By taking into account both the distance and the angle between the direction of movement and the vector connecting the positions of two pedestrians, the repulsive force in the SFM can be refined to better capture the complexities of real-world pedestrian flow scenarios [1][3]. This approach allows for a more accurate description of macroscopic pedestrian flow, enabling the evaluation of escape routes, the design of pedestrian facilities, and the study of other safety-critical aspects of crowd dynamics [3].

The SFM allows for the simulation of pedestrian behavior and the prediction of crowd movement in different scenarios, such as evacuation from a building.
Over the years, it has undergone various modifications and enhancements to improve its accuracy in simulating pedestrian dynamics and to address its difficulties in describing certain scenarios (see subproblems).

From a numerical point of view, an advantage of this subclass of models is that it has no singularity at contact of two pedestrians.

Section: Introduction

Recent experimental evidence from a variety of living neural networks suggests that the brain may be operating at or near a critical point, poised between disordered (“subcritical”) and ordered (“supercritical”) phases where cascades of activity are damped or amplified, respectively, . At this interface, neural networks are expected to produce avalanches of activity whose size and duration probability distributions follow power laws, as a distinctive feature of critical phenomena is scale-invariance, . Theory and simulations conjectured that neural networks poised at a critical point would have optimal information transmission , information storage, computational power, dynamic range, and learning capabilities , while providing flexible, yet stable dynamics , . Several experiments claim results consistent with these predictions, lending plausibility to the criticality hypothesis of brain function .Here we introduce and analyze the so-called cortical branching model (CBM), a non-equilibrium stochastic cellular automaton capturing many features of neural network data, and develop an analytical mean-field approximation in the form of an autonomous nonlinear discrete dynamical map of first order and dimension given by the integer-valued refractory period. We establish the non-equilibrium phase diagram of the CBM and identify three separate phases: the disordered, the ordered, and the quasiperiodic phases. Using this mean-field approximation, we argue that a continuous phase transition between the disordered and ordered phases occurs (in the thermodynamic limit) only when external driving, which we model as the spontaneous activation of network elements, is absent.In our CBM, when external driving is present (a key feature of open dynamical systems), we find that this phase transition disappears and hence argue that true criticality is not attainable by living neural networks. We thus introduce an extension, along with a more proper quantitative formulation of the quasi-criticality hypothesis. Our quasi-criticality hypothesis involves a non-equilibrium Widom line of maximum (though finite) dynamical susceptibility along which correlation length and, as we shall demonstrate, mutual information are maximized. Moreover, universal properties of the transition would eclipse the relevance of the details of the properties of individual neurons and their interactions , meaning that certain features of brain dynamics could be described by much simpler models. The cortical branching model (CBM) is one such model which has successfully reproduced many dynamical features of living brain tissue, . expected_output: The fixed points of the PCA-EP algorithm are eigenvectors of a specific matrix, and since the asymptotic performance of PCA-EP can be characterized via the SE platform, it is conceivable that the fixed points of the SE describe the asymptotic performance of the spectral estimator. However, the relationship between the fixed points of PCA-EP and the asymptotic behavior of spectral estimators in terms of convergence rates and stability is still unclear and requires further analysis to determine if they correspond to the largest eigenvalue and how the free parameter should be chosen to achieve optimal performance.
actual_output: The fixed points of PCA-EP coincide with an eigenvector with a particular eigenvalue of the data matrix which the spectral estimator uses, as indicated by the fact that the fixed point of an expectation-propagation type algorithm called PCA-EP coincides with an eigenvector with a particular eigenvalue of the data matrix [1]. In high dimensional spiked covariance models, the asymptotic behaviors of empirical eigenvalues and eigenvectors depend on the interplay of spike magnitude of leading eigenvalues, dimensionality, and sample size, which affects the convergence rates and stability of the estimators [2]. input: How can graph-based methods and cylinder fitting be utilized to enhance bowel tracking, and what is the process for integrating these techniques to improve accuracy in medical imaging?
expected_output: Graph-based methods and cylinder fitting can be utilized to enhance bowel tracking by constructing a bowel graph based on wall detection and computing the minimum cost path between given start and end nodes. The proposed framework builds upon existing methods, but with a new cost function facilitated by local cylinder fitting, which aims to improve accuracy in tracking the entire course of the small bowel from routine CT scans. The process for integrating these techniques involves first visualizing intestinal segments using 3D volume rendering, where each segment is colored based on the distance from an endpoint along the running path of each intestinal segment. Constrained distance transformation is then utilized to find endpoints of an intestinal segment, and cylinder fitting is applied to facilitate the cost function in the graph-based method. By combining these techniques, the enhanced graph-based method can achieve a high recall throughout the entire small bowel, while reducing errors from wall detection, ultimately improving accuracy in medical imaging.
actual_output: A new graph-based method for small bowel path tracking utilizes the fact that the bowel is a tube by fitting piecewise cylinders along its course and guiding the tracking to follow their orientation, which helps to overcome difficulties such as contact between parts of itself and the indistinct appearance of the wall [1]. This method finds the minimum cost path on a graph constructed based on wall detection and applies an explicit constraint implemented by must-pass nodes to better cover the entire course of the small bowel [2]. The integration of cylinder fitting into the graph-based method prevents tracking from crossing walls at contact areas and improves the accuracy of bowel tracking, as evidenced by clear improvements over baseline methods in terms of maximum length of the ground truth path tracked without error [3]. The quality of small bowel segmentation affects the path tracking outcome, and the proposed method benefits from excluding segmentation errors, making its advantages more evident [3].

Section: Discussion

We have presented a new graph-based method for small bowel path tracking. We find the minimum cost path on a graph constructed based on the wall detection. A new graph-based method for small bowel path tracking was presented. input: What are the limitations of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) in non-homogeneous media, and how do these limitations impact their performance compared to traditional methods introduced in earlier works?
expected_output: The limitations of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) in non-homogeneous media include the requirement for a large number of neurons in the hidden layer to effectively learn complex nonlinear patterns, which can increase exponentially with the complexity and non-linearity of the model. Additionally, the performance of DNNs strongly relies on the configuration of the neural network and the optimization algorithms used, such as the choice of activation functions and optimization algorithms. If not properly selected, these configurations can negatively impact the learning ability of the DNNs. Furthermore, the number of hidden layers and the number of neurons in each layer can significantly affect the performance of the DNNs in solving PDEs. However, recent studies have shown that DNNs can render better approximations for nonlinear functions compared to traditional methods, and researchers have developed various deep learning-based numerical methods to solve PDEs, including physics-informed neural networks and deep learning-based collocation methods. Despite these limitations, DNNs have been shown to be effective in solving PDEs in non-homogeneous media, and their performance can be improved with the optimal selection of neural network configurations and optimization algorithms.
actual_output: The limitations of Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) in solving Partial Differential Equations (PDEs) in non-homogeneous media include relatively low accuracy of the solutions, with absolute error rarely going below the level of 10^{-3} to 10^{-4}, as seen in Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) [1]. Additionally, PINNs require substantial computational resources and training time, making them less practical for large-scale or complex problems, and their training often encounters difficulties when target solutions involve sharp gradients or discontinuities [1][2]. These limitations impact the performance of DNNs compared to traditional methods, such as finite element method (FEM), which DNN-based methods aim to overcome due to the curse of dimensionality of traditional PDE solvers [3]. Furthermore, the training of DNNs for solving PDEs is computationally intensive and can lead to memory constraints, highlighting the need for more efficient and robust methods [4].

Paper: Deep Petrov-Galerkin Method for Solving Partial Differential Equations
Section: Introduction

Deep neural networks (DNNs) have achieved great success in artificial intelligence, scientific computing and other machine learning tasks (, ). DNNs produce a large class of nonlinear functions through compositional construction. Due to their powerful universal approximation ability, in recent years, DNNs have been applied for solving partial differential equations (PDEs), and several DNN-based methods (, ) were proposed to overcome the difficulty so-called the “curse of dimensionality" of the traditional PDE solvers such as finite element method (FEM), which requires a discretization of the interested domain, while the number of the mesh points will increase exponentially fast with respect to the problem dimension and make it quickly become computationally intractable. In such a situation, the generation of meshes is very time-consuming as well.Among these DNN-based methods, one approach is to establish the algorithm with the strong form and minimize the residual of the original PDEs, such as physical informed neural networks (PINNs), deep Galerkin method (DGM), mixed residual method (MIM), local extreme learning machines (locELM) and so on. Specifically, PINN was proposed in to use neural networks to approximate the solution of PDEs, and the neural networks are trained by minimizing the mean squared errors of the residual of the observed data, the differential equation, boundary conditions, and/or initial conditions. After that, some other model variants, like fractional PINNs and nonlocal PINNs are put forward in, . DGM designs the loss function as PDE residual in the least-square sense to measure how well the approximate solution satisfies the differential operator and boundary conditions (). Random symmetric matrices have Betti curves that are consistent and similar in organization, indicating that most matrix orderings have a similar arrangement of cliques. In contrast, geometric matrices, which are obtained as the distance matrix of sample points randomly distributed on a manifold, have Betti curves that are dramatically different due to the non-uniform sampling of possible matrix orderings. expected_output:
The advantages of using Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs) over Fully Connected Neural Networks (FCNNs) in feature extraction tasks are primarily due to their ability to respect translation symmetry and extract local features explicitly. CNNs achieve this through the use of convolutional layers, which apply filters to small regions of the input data, allowing them to capture local patterns and features. This is particularly beneficial in tasks where the data has spatial or temporal hierarchies, such as image or signal processing. In contrast, FCNNs treat all input data equally, without considering spatial or temporal relationships, which can lead to poor performance in tasks that require the extraction of local features.

The advantages of CNNs over FCNNs impact their performance in practice in several ways. Firstly, CNNs are able to achieve higher accuracy in feature extraction tasks, as they are able to capture local patterns and features more effectively. This is evident in the context, where the CNN outperforms the FCNN in predicting winding numbers, even in cases where the winding numbers are larger than those seen during training. Secondly, CNNs are able to generalize better to new, unseen data, as they are able to extract features that are invariant to translation and other transformations. This is demonstrated in the context, where the CNN is able to predict winding numbers accurately, even in cases where the input data is different from that seen during training.

Furthermore, the use of convolutional layers in CNNs allows for the extraction of features at multiple scales, which can be beneficial in tasks where the data has multiple spatial or temporal hierarchies. This is evident in the context, where the CNN is able to extract features from the input data at multiple scales, allowing it to predict winding numbers accurately. In contrast, FCNNs are limited in their ability to extract features at multiple scales, as they treat all input data equally.

Overall, the advantages of CNNs over FCNNs in feature extraction tasks make them a more effective choice for a wide range of applications, including image and signal processing, natural language processing, and more. Their ability to respect translation symmetry, extract local features explicitly, and generalize well to new data make them a powerful tool for extracting relevant features from complex data.

Evaluating and comparing topic models has always been a challenging task in research, due to the unsupervised nature of the models. The most widely used evaluation metric in recent topic modeling literature is topic coherence, which computes how the top-n words of a topic are related to each other . A topic is 'coherent' when it displays words that tend to occur in the same documents. There are multiple different coherence measures, from which the normalized pointwise mutual information (NPMI) measure has the largest correlation to human judgment of how coherent a topic is . NPMI ranges from [-1, 1], where a higher positive NPMI means that words within a topic are more related, which is desirable.
Topic coherence metrics are frequently combined with diversity metrics , . Topic diversity is defined as the percentage of unique words in the top-n words of all topics. The measure ranges from [0,1], where a topic diversity close to 0 indicates redundant topics and diversity close to 1 indicates more varied topics, which is desirable. However, since there is no 'ground truth' in the evaluation of unsupervised models, these measures should only be used as proxies for a topic model's performance.Another method to evaluate topic model performance is by means of human judgment . However, a problem with human judgment is that it is subjective: one annotator might judge the quality of a topic differently from another annotator. Moreover, human judgment is unreliable when comparing different topic modeling algorithms, as topic interpretability by humans does not necessarily mean that the actual topic modeling task was performed well. To illustrate, centroid-based topic representations, such as Top2Vec , could result in better human evaluations than other algorithms. This is not due to the actual topic model performance but simply because the words in a topic that are shown are synonyms, as these are the words close to a cluster's centroid. Showing a topic that contains several synonyms could result in bias as people think the topic is of higher quality.

Most objects with temperatures above absolute zero emit a notable amount of IR radiation, as outlined by . Such sources are all around us. In the creation of IR images, a substantial portion of the signals consist of radiated emissions. One notable advantage of these emissions is their persistent presence and their ability to withstand deterioration caused by adverse weather conditions. These characteristics make the IR spectrum a practical wavelength for imaging, especially in applications related to defense.
The origins of IR radiation can be traced back to a scientific experiment conducted by Frederick William Herschel over two centuries ago. Herschel used prisms and basic temperature sensors to study the distribution of wavelengths across the electromagnetic spectrum. It is now widely accepted that objects emit radiation across a wide spectrum of wavelengths, following established principles of physics. Within the electromagnetic spectrum, the infrared (IR) region spans wavelengths from 700 nanometers to 1 millimeter, with the lower end coinciding with the red edge of the visible spectrum. Empirical evidence shows that a significant portion of the IR spectrum is unsuitable for conventional applications due to the absorption of IR radiation by atmospheric water or carbon dioxide , . This IR range is conventionally divided into five spectral sub-bands. The near-infrared (NIR) spectrum covers wavelengths from 0.7 µm to 0.9 µm, while the shortwave IR (SWIR) ranges from 0.9 µm to 2.5 µm. The mid-wave infrared (MWIR) spectrum includes wavelengths between 3 µm and 5 µm, and the long-wave infrared (LWIR) spectrum comprises wavelengths from 8 µm to 12 µm. Lastly, the far-infrared (FIR) spectrum extends to wavelengths of up to 1000 micrometers.

Network analysis is an effective way to gain insight into different aspects of complex systems, which derives many machine learning applications, such as the online advertisement targeting and anomaly detection . Hence, identifying effective features of nodes (or edges) in a network is essential. However, traditional methods tend to manually mine the specific domain features depending on the expert experience, which not only require the high cost of labor and time, but also limit the scalability of models on different prediction tasks . Network representation learning (NRL) as an alternative of automatic feature mining has been proved to be beneficial to various network analysis tasks, such as the node classification , link prediction , clustering and visualization.Early NRL methods are mostly based on the matrix factorization. To reduce the computational complexity on large-scale networks, inspired by word modeling, Perozzi et al. propose DeepWalk.
Notably, the above-mentioned shallow model design cannot well capture the highly non-linearity that is universal in the networks, which would lead to the sub-optimal network representation . Then, many deep models, such as structural deep network embedding (SDNE), have emerged.Considering only the network structure is not enough to learn the informative and accurate node representations, especially when the network structure is sparse. Social science theories like the homophily and social influence theory suggest that there is a strong correlation between the structure and the attributes. Therefore, many studies focus on attributed NRL , which mainly learn the consistent node representations from the network structure and node attributes. Nevertheless, the above models are likely susceptible to the sparsity of one of the
heterogeneous information sources. Afterwards, the deep coupling paradigm is introduced to enhance the robustness of the representations. Attributed network representation learning (ANRL) is one of the representative examples. However, the ANRL model could be affected by the characteristics of the local network structure. In addition, the previous attributed NRL methods rarely preserve all the microscopic structural information, i.e., the first-order, second-order, and high-order proximity, together, where these proximities indicate the one-step, two-step, and multi-step relationship between two nodes. Since there is no measurable parameter that enables unequivocal age determination, various methods have been developed to estimate stellar population ages using different indicators. These include asteroseismology , evaporation ages , gyrochronology, kinematic and traceback ages, lithium depletion (boundary) measurements, or lithium equivalent widths . However, these methods all share a “specialist” limitation, in that they may only be suited for specific age, temperature, or mass ranges, require precise, work-intensive observed parameters, or can only be applied to either individual stars or ensembles. .Contrasting these rather specialized methods with narrow application ranges is an approach often praised for its generalistic nature – isochrone fitting. Based on variants of the Hertzsprung-Russel diagram, particularly the color-absolute magnitude diagram (CMD), it is a popular estimation technique with only minimal observational data requirements. As a result of Gaia providing photometry and astrometry for billions of sources, isochrone fitting has become perhaps the most used approach to age determination to date. Because of its connection to the HRD, the method is widely applicable across stellar age and mass ranges, for example from 0.5 Myr to 10 Gyr for M_* = 0.01 - 1.4~M_{\odot } or 10 Myr to 12.5 Gyr for M_* = 0.09 - 14~M_{\odot } . There are two major drawbacks to fitting isochrones, though: On the one hand, it heavily relies on the specific physics considered when modeling the theoretical isochrones. As the different physical processes of stellar evolution are highly complex and vary between different stellar ages and masses , this translates into a large number of free parameters, which can produce systematic errors in age estimates across different stellar evolution models and prior assumptions. Given the many different available stellar evolution codes for model isochrones, such as BHAC15 , DSEP-magnetic , BT-Settl , PARSEC, MIST , and BaSTI, this dependence has a profound impact on age estimates found in literature. On the other hand, the fitting technique of the isochrones to the CMD data itself can strongly impact the results. From the observational side, measurement errors and incomplete or contaminated cluster member data are drivers of age uncertainties .Additionally, observational cluster CMDs include an unknown amount of unresolved binary stars. The extent of this contaminating population has been estimated to range from about 29 to 50 % , and equal mass unresolved binaries reside at the maximum possible displacement of -0.753mag above the main sequence. Additionally, reddening effects of non-equal mass unresolved binaries have been found to cause a shift of the corresponding data points closer, or right onto, the equal mass binary sequence , . Consequently, it often appears disproportionately enlarged compared to the expected number of equal mass binaries. The presence of such a well-defined locus of contaminants harbors another challenge to isochronal age determination. However, the impact of the binary sequence on the empirical isochrones presented in this work has been specifically addressed and quantified (see Appendix .Consequently, it is challenging to verify age estimates obtained through different age estimation methods or to establish a uniform age for an object using the literature, . In the following paragraphs, we examine this situation's implications, focusing on isochrone fitting.

Paper: Ages of stars: Methods and uncertainties
Section: Discussion

Isochrones are loci of constant age computed from stellar models. Those models are fundamentally calibrated against the Sun, with further refinement from matching details of cluster H-R diagrams. Fitting isochrones to clusters to determine an age involves using a distribution of stars of many masses, even for sparse clusters or groups. Even then, fitting the turn-off region can be challenging because there may be only a few stars or the presence of binaries among them may be unappreciated.One works with less information in placing individual stars in HRDs and so the uncertainties are greater. As an example, showed a synthetic study of isochrone placement for F stars. They took stars of a variety of masses and ages from about 1.2[FORMULA] on up, added realistic estimates of errors in luminosity and temperature, and then tested how well the original ages could be recovered. A significant problem in using isochrones is that they are not evenly spaced in the HRD, leading to biased results. Of the methods they tried, that using Bayesian techniques worked the best because that takes account of prior information about isochrone spacing. For fairly well-evolved stars above 1.2[FORMULA] , the age errors were as small as 20%, but were more typically 50% for most stars. These are large for individual stars but could be acceptable for ensembles where averaging will reduce the uncertainty. Another limitation of the Bayesian method is that one ends up with a probability distribution function (PDF), not a specific value. In many cases the PDF is single-peaked, but there are instances when the PDFs have multiple peaks or give only upper- or lower limits, and, depending on how those are used they can distort or bias an average.Isochrone placement remains the most favored technique for more massive stars ([FORMULA] , say), where the relative errors are modest.

We fit model isochrones to the 37 extracted SigMA clusters to infer cluster ages. Isochronal age estimates are an effective tool for studying relative ages and age sequences in the CMD, as consistent shifts in the position of pre–main-sequence (PMS) objects relative to the main-sequence (MS), precise photometry, and parallax measurements from Gaia provide reliable evidence for relative age differences between populations. These systematic shifts are especially pronounced in young populations (\le 100 Myr). As older populations reach the main sequence, the changes in the isochrones below the turn-off become almost imperceptible due to the long-lasting, stable process of hydrogen burning, which keeps the CMD distribution virtually stagnant .Although relative age sequences become apparent when comparing young populations in the CMD, determining absolute ages is a process that is prone to biasing effects of systematic uncertainties. Such uncertainties, for instance, arise from the use of different isochronal model families . To mitigate the systematic effect of different evolutionary models on our method, we employ two model families: PARSEC and BHAC15 (Sect. ).Another systematic uncertainty is introduced by the choice of the fitting technique itself, as different fitting approaches are accompanied by disparate assumptions about the underlying data distribution of the measurements. For example, the popular and often used least squares (LS) method is based on the expectation that the data exhibit Gaussian uncertainties around the regression curve.
However, assuming a Gaussian distribution of the data may not be entirely justified in the first place, as it is well-established that observational trends such as the unresolved binary sequence appear brighter compared to the single-star main sequence. At the same time, extinction skews the source distribution towards fainter magnitudes and redder colors. As a result, a fit of the (bluer) left-main ridge of the data in the CMD is often the preferred location for an isochrone, as it is believed to represent the underlying data more accurately. This can, for example, be achieved with fitting techniques that do not implicitly assume Gaussian distribution (see Sect. REF ).As susceptibility to outliers is a general problem (and not specifically related to LS), we aim to curb their influence by applying photometric quality filters (see Sect.  for a detailed outline of the applied quality criteria) and employing robust fitting techniques. Robust fitting techniques are less sensitive to the influence of outliers in the data . As we still observed outliers in the CMD distributions after applying our quality cuts, we aim to use techniques that decrease their influence, producing more stable and reliable results. In the following, we briefly discuss robust methods and the choice of an appropriate method depending on the specific characteristics of the data.

Paper: Towards Better Age Estimates for Stellar Populations: The Y^2 Isochrones for Solar Mixture
Section: Introduction

Isochrones are defined as the locus of coeval (equal age) points on
the evolutionary tracks of stars of different masses in the
Hertzsprung-Russell Diagram (HRD).
An older isochrone has a fainter and redder main-sequence
turn-off (MSTO), because the brighter and bluer massive stars evolve and die
earlier.
For the past four decades, astronomers have used this basic fact in
various ways to derive the ages of star clusters and galaxies.The first systematic application of the isochrone method was made
to NGC 188 MSTO by Demarque and Larson (1964), as noted by Sandage and Eggen
(1969).
The widespread adoption of the isochrone technique has been
tremendously helpful in understanding the formation and evolution of the Milky
Way and its components, and the chronological sequence of astrophysical
processes therein (see VandenBerg, Bolte, & Stetson 1996;
Sarajedini, Chaboyer, & Demarque 1997).
Today, isochrones are the most powerful means of measuring
the ages of star clusters, and thanks to numerous recent improvements
in the input physics, we may now claim to know the age of the Milky Way
better than ever before.
This purely theoretical achievement helps setting one of the
most important constraints on cosmology, because the age of the
universe is a distinctive product of any cosmological model.A second-generation isochrone technique extends beyond
the MSTO up to the tip of the red giant branch (RGB), to match more stars in
the HRD (Iben 1974; Demarque & McClure 1977).
The use of the extended isochrone, now standard, confers at least
two significant advantages over the use of only the MSTO.
Firstly, isochrone fitting is no longer in principle sensitive to
the uncertainty in distance measurement.
This advantage, however, has not practically been much appreciated
because the uncertainties in the stellar atmosphere models
and in the convection approximations still make it difficult to reproduce
accurately the colors of red giants.
Secondly, it allows us to build realistic population models for
clusters and galaxies from their initial mass functions.
This technique, called “evolutionary population synthesis” (EPS),
was pioneered by Tinsley (1980).In spite of the attendant difficulties, attempts to reproduce the colors
and spectra of clusters and galaxies through the EPS technique are increasingly
successful, and especially so when empirical stellar spectral libraries are
resorted to (eg. Larson and Tinsley 1978; Gunn, Stryker, & Tinsley 1981;
Bruzual 1983; Pickles 1985).
The usage of isochrones has increased steadily.
Notably, the recent studies of Spinrad et al. (1997) and
Yi et al. (2000) have demonstrated that precision-isochrones can be used to
constrain the galaxy formation epoch directly by estimating the
ages of high-redshift galaxies in their youth.
Such studies have demonstrated that population synthesis
studies with precision-isochrones may even differentiate between various
cosmological models.Isochrones need to be updated when significant improvements are made
in input physics. The Yale group (eg. Green, Demarque, & King 1987) is one
among several involved in such activity.
Other notable recent updates include Schaller et al. (1992),
Straniero, Chieffi, & Limongi (1997), Girardi et al. (2000), and
VandenBerg et al. (2000).
The Yale group's prior published set of isochrones, the Revised Yale
Isochrones (: hereafter RYI), are out-of-date.

input: What is the process for adapting TTRS to open-source software, and how can TTRC's approach be applied to achieve this adaptation?
expected_output: The process for adapting Time To Restore Service (TTRS) to open-source software involves modifying the metric to Time To Repair Code (TTRC), which measures the time it takes to release a new version of the code that includes changes that correct bugs. To achieve this adaptation, the TTRC approach can be applied by calculating the time difference between the moment a bug issue is raised and the moment the changes that solve the bug are released in a new version of the code. This is done by defining a formula that sums up the time differences for each bug and then dividing by the total number of bugs reported during a period of time. The result is the mean time to repair code, which can be used to evaluate the stability of open-source software projects. Additionally, the standard deviation of the time to repair code can be calculated to reflect the variations in the time it takes to solve different bugs, providing further insight into the project's stability.

Additionally, the development of TTS systems based on speaking styles, such as normal TTS, Lombard TTS, SSDRC TTS, and Lombard-SSDRC TTS, can be used to adapt TTRS to open-source software, with each module trained separately using data from the corresponding target speech style [2].

Paper: Test-time Adaptation for Cross-modal Retrieval with Query Shift
Section: Introduction

Test-time Adaptation (TTA) has emerged as a promising avenue for domain adaptation, which aims to reconcile the distribution shifts in an online manner.
Towards achieving this goal, some Test-Time Training (TTT) approaches, have been proposed, which require modifying the training process of the source model and adding an auxiliary self-supervised task.
As a result, the source model could be adapted by performing the self-supervised task on the online target data stream.
To avoid the reduplicated training cost of the source model, Fully Test-Time Adaptation  paradigm has been proposed, which could be coarsely divided into the following three categories: i) online TTA methods, which continually update the normalization layers by resorting to the unsupervised objectives, such as entropy minimization or its variants. ii) robust TTA methods, which strive to improve the robustness against noisy predictions, mixed distribution shifts, label shifts, and so on. iii) TTA beyond recognition, which focuses on the tasks including but not limited to image restoration , multimodal recognition , and multimodal segmentation .In this paper, we focus on online TTA for achieving robust cross-modal retrieval against query shift.
Among existing approaches, DISC  is most relevant to our work, while having significantly different motivations.
In brief, DISC is designed to adapt the pre-trained image hashing models against the distribution shift for achieving effective retrieval in the target domain.
Different from DISC, our work focuses on addressing the query shift problem for cross-modal retrieval, which is less-touched by the existing studies.
Moreover, unlike DISC that requires accessing the source data to train the hashing model, our TCR could adapt the off-the-shelf pre-trained models without using the source data.
[Figure: Overview of the proposed TCR.For the given online queries, the modality-specific encoders are employed to project the query and gallery samples into the latent space established by the source model.The obtained query embeddings and gallery embeddings are passed into the query prediction refinement module.In the module, TCR first selects the most similar gallery sample for each query and obtain the query-gallery pairs.After that, the pairs with higher uniformity and lower modality gap are chosen to estimate the filtering threshold of query predictions and modality gap of the source model as the constraints for the adaptation.Finally, three loss functions are employed to achieve robust adaptation for cross-modal retrieval with query shift.]

input: What is the process for applying wavelength and flat-field calibrations to grism spectra in a way that ensures accurate and reliable results across different observational settings?
expected_output: The process for applying wavelength and flat-field calibrations to grism spectra involves several steps to ensure accurate and reliable results. First, the wavelengths in the grism spectrum are calculated using coefficients recommended by STScI, with modifications as needed to achieve optimal agreement between the observed spectra and known profiles. The coefficients are varied by up to 10% through trial-and-error to obtain good consistency of the grism response and accounting of stellar absorption lines. Additionally, a wavelength-dependent flat field calibration is applied as recommended by STScI, which is a function of where each target's spectrum falls on the detector and must be done at the user stage of data analysis. However, if the stellar spectra are fixed on the detector during each visit and jitter and drift in wavelength are negligible, flat-fielding may not be necessary. The entire analysis can be repeated without the flat-fielding step to verify consistent results, and this step is prudent in cases where wavelength jitter in spatial scan mode can be larger than in non-scanned observations. Overall, the application of wavelength and flat-field calibrations requires careful consideration of the observational settings and the specific characteristics of the data to ensure accurate and reliable results.
actual_output: The process for applying wavelength and flat-field calibrations to grism spectra involves a wavelength-dependent correction, where flat-field calibration is applied as a correction but is not included in the standard STScI pipeline processing [1]. Wavelength calibration of grism spectra is performed using coefficients recommended by STScI, with modifications to achieve optimal agreement between observed and known grism response profiles and stellar absorption line wavelengths, which is crucial for accurate results [1]. A grism flat-field cube is constructed via interpolation of flat-fields from different imaging filters using a 3rd order polynomial function of pixel coordinates and wavelength, allowing for field and wavelength dependent corrections due to varying source positions in direct images [2]. The wavelength calibration process relies on a pair of direct and grism images, where the zero point is set by the object's position in the direct image, and background subtraction is performed before flux summation in each wavelength bin, including corrections for flatfield imprint and enhanced dark current [3][4]. Overall, the calibration process for grism spectra requires careful consideration of wavelength-dependent corrections, flat-fielding, and background subtraction to ensure accurate and reliable results across different observational settings [1][2][4][3].

The use of linear and elliptic motions in the dataset is intended to simulate real-world video sequences, where object motion is typically smooth. The dataset's design allows for the evaluation of model performance based on metrics such as mean square error (MSE), peak signal-noise ratio (PSNR), and structure similarity (SSIM). The inclusion of linear and elliptic motions in the dataset can help improve model accuracy by providing a more realistic and challenging test environment. The elliptic motion, in particular, can help models learn to handle more complex and nuanced motion patterns. Overall, the use of linear and elliptic motions in the Moving-MNIST-2 dataset can have a positive impact on model performance, as it allows models to learn and generalize from a wider range of motion patterns, making them more robust and effective in real-world applications.

Moreover, the introduction of stochasticity in the Stochastic Moving-MNIST dataset, where the velocity is perturbed with random Gaussian noise ε at each time step, allows for more realistic motion simulations, although models perform better with N-Body-MNIST, which introduces inter-digit influence on top of the original trajectory [3][4]. Overall, the results suggest that incorporating linear and elliptic motions in Moving-MNIST-2 datasets can improve model accuracy, particularly when combined with stochasticity and inter-digit influence, leading to more realistic and effective spatio-temporal predictions [1].

The standard Moving-MNIST dataset contains handwritten digits sampled from the MNIST dataset moving and bouncing with a constant velocity (u_0, v_0) on the 64\times 64 image plane. In the context of functional analysis and optimization, the PS condition ensures that a sequence of approximate critical points of a functional converges to a genuine critical point. This is achieved by requiring that any sequence satisfying certain conditions, such as boundedness and gradient convergence, has a convergent subsequence. The key properties that make the PS condition effective include its ability to establish compactness, weak convergence, and strong convergence of sequences, which are essential in a wide range of mathematical frameworks, including calculus of variations, partial differential equations, and optimization theory. By leveraging these properties, the PS condition enables researchers to establish the existence of solutions to various problems, including those involving nonlinear equations and variational inequalities. Furthermore, the PS condition has been adapted and generalized to accommodate different mathematical settings, such as constrained optimization, non-smooth analysis, and infinite-dimensional spaces, making it a fundamental tool in modern mathematics.

expected_output: Dynamic anisotropy near cut-off frequencies in the context of elastic wave scattering exhibits distinct wave propagation characteristics compared to static anisotropy. In the vicinity of the cut-off frequencies, specifically at ω = √6 for pressure waves and ω = 3√2/2 for shear waves, the dispersion surfaces of the bulk lattice display non-circular slowness contours. These contours lead to preferential directions of wave propagation, resulting in dynamic anisotropy. This phenomenon is manifested in the scattered field through effects such as star-shaped scattered waveforms, negative reflection, and negative refraction. In contrast, static anisotropy refers to the directional dependence of material properties, which can also influence wave propagation. However, dynamic anisotropy near cut-off frequencies is a unique feature that arises from the topology of the dispersion surfaces and is not directly related to static material anisotropy. The dynamic anisotropy observed in this context is a consequence of the frequency-dependent behavior of the lattice, whereas static anisotropy is a property of the material itself, independent of frequency.

In contrast, static anisotropy does not exhibit this change in curvature, and numerical solutions highlight the difference between results obtained for static and dynamic anisotropy in deforming two-phase aggregates [3]. The dynamic anisotropy behavior is also visible in the cross-shaped anisotropic profile, which shows strong contrast between wavelength inside and outside the material, although this observation is made with low confidence [2].

input: How can antiferromagnetic magnon renormalization effects be understood across different filling ranges, and what methods can be employed to analyze these variations?
expected_output: Antiferromagnetic magnon renormalization effects can be understood across different filling ranges by analyzing the behavior of the magnon dispersion relations and the spin stiffness. The renormalization effects become more pronounced at long wavelengths, particularly at the Brillouin zone center, where the spin stiffness decreases with doping and increases with the interaction strength. To analyze these variations, methods such as inelastic neutron scattering (INS) measurements and perturbative expansions can be employed. INS measurements can provide direct information about the magnon dispersion relations, while perturbative expansions can be used to calculate the renormalization effects and the spin stiffness. Additionally, comparisons with experimental results from single crystals of antiferromagnetic heavy fermions, such as CeIn3, can help to validate the theoretical models and provide insight into the behavior of the magnon renormalization effects. By combining these methods, researchers can gain a deeper understanding of the antiferromagnetic magnon renormalization effects and their variations across different filling ranges.
actual_output: Antiferromagnetic magnon renormalization effects can be understood across different filling ranges by analyzing the convergence radius of the perturbative series, which is wider than naively expected and depends on electronic structure and filling-dependent coefficients [1]. The renormalization of magnon modes is influenced by the presence of an uncompensated magnetic moment at the AF/S interface, which induces an effective exchange field in the adjacent metal via the interface exchange interaction, as seen in the case of a thin-film antiferromagnetic insulator proximity to a thin metal layer [2]. The dressed magnon energies are quite sensitive to electron filling, with larger spin wave softening increasing monotonically with filling, and the bandwidth ratio can have a sizeable effect on renormalized magnon modes, especially for wavevectors away from Brillouin zone boundaries [3]. At half-filling, the renormalization of antiferromagnetic magnons reduces spin wave frequency with respect to bare magnons, with the effect growing with the ratio of correlation strength to bandwidth, and the convergence of the perturbative series for renormalized magnons is limited to a restricted range of this ratio when correlation is strong enough to polarize the conduction band antiferromagnetically [4].

It is proposed that measurements of the renormalized dispersion relations can provide direct information about the amplitude of the effective exchange field induced by the AF in the adjacent metal. Additionally, the introduction of Lagrange multipliers can lead to a more stable and optimally convergent method, as demonstrated in the analysis of LBB-unstable and LBB-stable velocity-pressure FE pairs.
